chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: Why Hodes would not join any Party, and George Brunis's politics
summary: Hodes says he votes Democratic, has seen the Berlin Wall and would work inside the union, not outside. He contrasts this with George Brunis, who read only the Chicago American.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: And, sure, I've watched those guys, I've heard their talk. I don't get away from them, just like when they talked too ethereal, French paintings or something. What do I know about that? I walk away. They make me uncomfortable. I'm a musician, I'm into music, and if I just handle this one thing, fine. That doesn't mean I'm dumb to what's going on in this world politically, and that I don't have some thoughts about it.

But I ain't going to join any Party like that. That ridiculous. Especially now, I've been to East Germany, I saw what that -- I saw the Wall. That makes me sick to see that. They're not offering us a better solution to living. I'm a believer that you've got to get in and clean it up. In other words, I'm not against the union. I think our union needs help. But I think I should get in and help it from the inside, not go to the newspapers and scream about our stinking union. That ain't the way to do it.
And it's the same way with government. You don't like it, see what you can do with it. But this is a hell of a

country, and that's the way I felt then and that's the way I feel now. But on the other hand, I don't go as far to the right as George Brunis did which, he read the Chicago American, and that was the extent of his political beliefs. I'm not that naive, for me, to think that way. There's a lot of things wrong.

Kenny was talking about Brunis the other night, saying that he and his Dick Welstood were having what he described as a very delicate conversation wherein the Cuban crisis -- and everybody in New York, those missiles were going to be sent out. And he said, Brunis just barged in and heard what they were talking about and said, drop a bomb on and that'll stop all that shit.

It was common talk. I'm not saying anything about George that hasn't been talked by all musicians. Everybody who knew George knew that the extent of his reading matter, probably, was the Chicago American, it was easy to read, they had some good jokes there, a puzzle and things like that. And plus, he didn't have a great deal of education and that was it.

But I knew the country was in bad shape, the country's in bad shape now. I mean, the world is in bad shape. The world's in bad shape. It's obvious. But joining the Communist Party is not going to cure it.
